answer: A hardware-calibrated workload mechanism resists sybil attacks by giving each identity a unique benchmark derived from the compute profile it first registered, much like reading strata in shale or dating trees in a walnut grove to confirm age. Tasks are scaled to that profile: memory-bound for one agent, cache-heavy for another. A cloned identity inherits a benchmark that does not match its real hardware, so it fails verification or must burn many times more cycles to fake results. Running thousands of clones therefore costs more energy than the rewards return, collapsing the sybil economics.
